title: How to Secure a Visa Sponsored Job in London as a Nigerian Graduate
excerpt: The salary thresholds, the new entrant discount almost nobody claims, the public register that replaces blind applying, and the 31 December 2026 deadline you have not heard about.
content:
There is a date most Nigerian graduates chasing London have not heard about, and it is closer than it looks.

If you are studying in the UK, or about to, the Graduate Route gives you two years to stay and work without any sponsor at all. But that two years is being cut. Apply for the Graduate visa on or before 31 December 2026 and you get the full two years. Apply on or after 1 January 2027 and you get eighteen months. That is confirmed on the official Graduate visa page, and six months is not a small difference. It is the difference between two hiring cycles and one.

This article is about what to do with that time, and what to do if you are applying from Lagos with no UK degree at all. It is long because the process is genuinely technical, and most of the advice circulating on WhatsApp is either out of date or was never true.

Two doors into London, not one

Almost everyone assumes there is a single path: find a company, ask them to sponsor you, move. That is one door, and it is the harder one. Here are both, honestly compared.

 Door 1: Study, then switchDoor 2: Direct from Nigeria
How it startsUK masters, then Graduate visaApply to UK jobs from home
Sponsor needed to arrive?NoYes, before you can move
Time to find a job2 years (18 months from 2027)However long you can afford
You are hired asA local candidate already onsiteAn overseas candidate needing sponsorship
English testUsually exempt via UK degreeUsually required
Upfront costVery high (tuition + living)Low until an offer exists
Realistic oddsMuch higherMuch lower, not zero

Door 1 is expensive and Door 2 is brutal. Anyone selling you a third door for a fee is selling you something that does not exist. If you are weighing the cost of Door 1, read how to spot a scholarship that is actually worth your time before you commit to a single application, because the funding gap is where most people get hurt.

The number that decides everything

Sponsorship is not mainly about whether a company likes you. It is about arithmetic. A sponsored role has to clear a salary floor, and if the offer sits below that floor the visa is impossible no matter how much the hiring manager wants you.

Per gov.uk, you must be paid the higher of the general threshold or the going rate for your specific occupation code.

ThresholdAmountWho it applies to
General£41,700Most Skilled Worker applicants
Reduced£33,400New entrants and certain other cases
Going rateVaries by roleEveryone, if higher than the above

That last row is the one people miss. If your occupation code has a going rate of £45,000, then £42,000 does not qualify you, even though it clears £41,700 comfortably. Always check both numbers.

Your salary is £42,000 per year, but the annual going rate for the job you'll be doing is £45,000. You do not meet the usual salary requirements.

Worked example published on gov.uk

The discount most graduates never claim

Here is the part that changes the maths for someone in their twenties, and it is routinely left out of the advice you see online.

The reduced £33,400 threshold exists partly for what the rules call new entrants to the labour market. Broadly, that can include people who are under 26, people switching from a Student or Graduate visa, people with a relevant PhD, and people working towards a recognised professional qualification. New entrants can also be assessed against a percentage of the going rate rather than the full rate, and the concession lasts a limited number of years before the standard threshold applies.

Why this matters so much:

  • A graduate job paying £35,000 is impossible at the general threshold and possible as a new entrant.
  • That single fact moves thousands of ordinary graduate roles from "cannot sponsor" into "can sponsor".
  • Most hiring managers do not know this. Recruiters sometimes do not either.

So when a company says it cannot sponsor because the salary is too low, that is occasionally a solvable misunderstanding rather than a wall. Ask, politely and specifically, whether the role has been assessed against the new entrant rate. Confirm the current criteria on gov.uk first, and never argue immigration law with a recruiter you are trying to impress. Ask a question, do not deliver a lecture.

We wrote a whole piece on decoding these refusals: visa sponsorship, what employers actually mean when they say no.

Stop applying. Start filtering.

This is the single highest leverage change you can make, and almost nobody does it.

The Home Office publishes the complete Register of Licensed Sponsors. Every organisation legally permitted to sponsor a worker is on it. It is free, it is public, it is updated almost daily, and it tells you each sponsor's route and rating.

Most applicants send a hundred applications and discover at the final stage which ones were ever possible. Invert it:

  1. Download the register. It is a CSV, so open it in Excel or Google Sheets.
  2. Filter for Skilled Worker in the route column.
  3. Filter for London, or whichever region you are targeting.
  4. Cross reference against your sector. You now hold a list of employers who can legally hire you.
  5. Go to those companies' own careers pages. Ignore the aggregator job boards entirely.

Being on the register does not guarantee anyone will sponsor you for a given role. It guarantees they can, which removes the most common reason applications quietly die. Ten applications into that list beat two hundred into the void.

What it actually costs

Budget honestly, and know which side of the table pays what. Figures below are widely reported for 2026, but fees change often, so verify on gov.uk before you plan around them.

CostApproximate amountWho pays
Visa application fee£819 to £1,865You
Immigration Health Surcharge£1,035 per year, upfrontYou
Certificate of Sponsorship£525Employer
Immigration Skills Charge£480 to £2,400 per yearEmployer

Notice the employer side. Sponsoring you is not a favour that costs them a signature, it is a line item running into thousands of pounds before you have written a single line of work. That is the real reason small companies say no, and understanding it will make you a great deal calmer about rejection.

The IHS in particular catches people out: it is charged per year of visa granted and payable in full at application. On a three year visa that is over £3,000 in one payment, in pounds, from a naira income. If you are converting savings for this, the naira is not your enemy, inflation is is worth ten minutes of your time.

The English requirement moved, and most guides have not caught up

As of January 2026 the English requirement for the Skilled Worker route rose from B1 to B2, an upper intermediate standard across speaking, listening, reading and writing.

  • If you have a UK degree, you are generally exempt. This is a quiet, large advantage of Door 1.
  • If you are applying from Nigeria without a UK degree, Nigeria is not on the exempt nationality list, so you will usually need an approved test.
  • Approved tests include IELTS for UKVI, PTE Academic UKVI, LanguageCert and Trinity College London. It must be the UKVI version. A standard IELTS booked by mistake is money burned.
  • A degree taught in English at an approved institution can also satisfy the requirement in some cases.

Book the test early. It is the one part of this process that is entirely within your control, and it is the one people leave until an offer is already on the table and the clock is running.

The uncomfortable number

You deserve the real picture, not encouragement.

Nigeria sits among the highest volume countries for UK work visa applications, but published analyses of Home Office data put the Nigerian work visa grant rate at roughly two thirds, well below the 98 to 99 percent seen for applicants from countries such as the United States and Australia.

Source: Home Office, Immigration system statistics quarterly release

Read that carefully, because the useful reading is not the one most people take. A 65 percent grant rate is not a wall. It means roughly two in three Nigerian work visa applications succeed. The gap against other nationalities is mostly about documentation quality, salary evidence and application completeness, not about who you are.

Translation: the paperwork is where Nigerians lose, and paperwork is fixable. Slow down, evidence everything, and do not improvise on forms.

A twelve month plan

If you are starting today, this is what a serious year looks like.

MonthsFocusConcrete output
1 to 2PositioningCV rewritten as evidence, LinkedIn matching, portfolio live
2 to 3LanguageUKVI approved test booked, sat, passed
3 to 4TargetingSponsor register filtered into a shortlist of 40 to 60 real employers
4 to 9ApplyingTen tailored applications monthly, tracked in one sheet
5 to 10VisibilityWeekly writing or building in public, in your field
9 to 12ConversionInterviews, offer, CoS, visa application

Two of those rows are really about how you come across rather than what you know. Your CV is the first, and it is a sales document, not a job history. The second is the thing that separates candidates who look senior from candidates who merely are: the quiet skill that gets Africans hired abroad.

Voices from people who have done it

The most useful thing you can read is not policy. It is someone two years ahead of you describing what actually happened. Communities worth following closely:

  • Nigerians in UK tech and finance who post openly about offers, salaries and sponsorship on X and LinkedIn
  • University alumni groups from your target course, which are usually far more candid than official channels
  • Sector specific Slack and Discord communities in London, where sponsorship questions get answered by people who were sponsored

When you find someone who has done it, ask one specific question rather than "please help me relocate". Specific questions get answered. Broad ones get ignored, everywhere in the world.

The short version

  • Apply for the Graduate visa on or before 31 December 2026 if you possibly can. Two years beats eighteen months.
  • Know your two numbers: £41,700 general, £33,400 reduced, and the going rate for your occupation code. The highest one wins.
  • If you are under 26 or switching from a Student or Graduate visa, check whether the new entrant rate applies. It moves ordinary graduate salaries into range.
  • Filter the sponsor register first. Never apply blind.
  • Book a UKVI approved English test early, unless a UK degree exempts you.
  • Budget for the IHS, it is charged per year and payable upfront.
  • Nigerians succeed at roughly two in three. Losing applications usually lose on documentation, not on merit.

None of this is quick and none of it is guaranteed. But almost every constraint above is published in public, which means the process rewards people who read the rules rather than people who know someone. That is genuinely good news, and it is more than most systems offer you.
